query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build-plate during Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder to an optimal temperature range (300–500 °C) will slow down the cooling rate during solidification, leading to a more homogeneous microstructure with reduced compositional segregation, lower residual thermal stresses, and fewer defects, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity by at least 20% over conventionally processed parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powder as used in standard L-PBF processing.
generation.intervention: Introduce a build-plate preheating stage that elevates the substrate temperature to approximately 300–500 °C during layer-by-layer additive manufacturing.
generation.conditions: Processing via L-PBF in an inert atmosphere with typical industry-standard laser power, scan speed, and layer thickness; valid for conditions where cooling rates and thermal gradients are similar to those encountered in conventional builds.
generation.structural_mediator: More controlled solidification kinetics leading to refined, uniform grain structures, minimized compositional gradients at layer boundaries, and reduced formation of thermal stress-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build plate lowers the thermal gradient between the melt pool and substrate, which slows the cooling rate and reduces the driving force for element segregation and rapid stress buildup. This controlled cooling promotes a more uniform microstructure and fewer defects compared to rapid solidification conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: At least a 20% improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility) along with measurable reductions in compositional segregation and residual stress compared to parts fabricated without build-plate preheating.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi parts fabricated by conventional L-PBF processing with an unheated (room temperature) build plate.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under standard L-PBF conditions (e.g., inert atmosphere, typical laser parameters, and layer thickness) and may not hold if processing parameters or alloy systems deviate significantly from these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (e.g., the 20% value) is an estimate based on analogous systems and machine learning predictions; sensitivity to preheat temperature variation and part geometry introduces some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples by L-PBF under identical processing parameters except for the build-plate temperature. One set will be produced using a room-temperature build plate (control) and the other set using a preheated build plate at 300–500 °C. Post-build, assess microstructural homogeneity (via SEM and EDS), residual stress levels (using X-ray or neutron diffraction), mechanical integrity (using tensile and fatigue tests), and defect density (via X-ray computed tomography).
measurements: Grain structure and segregation mapping via SEM and EDS
Residual stress quantification via XRD or neutron diffraction
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility) via tensile and fatigue testing
Defect analysis using X-ray computed tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated build-plate samples do not show statistically significant improvements in microstructural uniformity, reduced residual stress, and at least ~20% enhanced mechanical properties compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Selective laser melting (SLM) is one of the additive manufacturing technologies that has been recognized as an affordable and efficient solution to manufacture complex metal parts with near full density. In SLM processing, a controllable intensive laser beam was used to selectively fully melt and solidify the metal powder bed in a layer-by-layer manner according to the scanning strategy provided by the sliced computer aided design (CAD) file. The unique building method and relatively high cooling rate of SLM made it possible to manufacture parts with complex shapes and form unique microstructures to produce excellent mechanical properties, which could not be easily obtained by traditional methods [,,]. As a new class of metallic materials, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have spurred great interest since they were proposed [,]. In contrast to traditional alloy design strategy, high-entropy alloys consist of five or more multiple principle elements mixed in an equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratio. frame.system: A cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy fabricated from powder feedstock intended for additive manufacturing.
frame.goal: To improve mechanical integrity while simultaneously limiting segregation, residual thermal stresses, and defect formation relative to conventional processing methods.
frame.limitation: Conventional bulk processing and standard additive manufacturing routes elicit compositional segregation during cooling and generate residual stresses that compromise mechanical performance.
constraints: use of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock
improvement must be realized without introducing additional cost or further complicating processing
frame.regime: Processing via additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) under controlled atmosphere, with experimental validation limited to the processing and testing conditions typical for bulk and AM parts (e.g., temperature ranges, cooling rates, and stress states encountered during standard builds).
prior_attempts: Bulk fabrication methods that induce segregation upon slow cooling
Mainstream metallic additive manufacturing techniques that result in residual thermal stresses and processing defects
frame.understanding: The proposed intervention exploits controlled thermal management during the manufacturing process to tailor the solidification kinetics. Specifically, preheating the build substrate is hypothesized to reduce the thermal gradients during solidification, thereby mitigating rapid local cooling that leads to compositional segregation, lowering residual stress accumulation, and reducing defect formation.
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a build-plate preheating stage (for example, elevating the substrate temperature to an optimal range such as 300–500 °C) during additive manufacturing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will slow down the cooling rate. This controlled solidification is expected to reduce compositional segregation along with residual stresses and defects, yielding at least a 20% improvement in mechanical integrity compared to parts fabricated by conventional methods. The hypothesis is applicable under typical AM conditions (e.g., using laser powder bed fusion in an inert atmosphere) and can be falsified by a decisive experiment: manufacturing comparable sets of samples with and without preheating and quantitatively correlating microstructural homogeneity (by, e.g., scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive spectroscopy), residual stress (by X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction), and mechanical properties (via tensile or fatigue testing). Failure to observe the predicted improvements would falsify the hypothesis.
